nodes.text: Encrypted chats still trust providers; only client-held keys minimize that trust.

evidence.text: E2EE definition: encrypted on sender device, decrypted on receiver device, never decrypted in transit. Against men-in-the-middle most implementations suffice; but users usually want no outsider, especially the provider, reading content. WhatsApp metadata (network, frequency, volume, timing) still aids interpretation.

Core lesson: trust rests on reputation, jurisdiction, business model, behavior, not verifiable guarantees. Attack surface shrinks WhatsApp to Proton to Signal recovery keys (device or key compromise only).
Bottom line: prefer client-side encryption, open-source everything, decentralized minimal-trust systems, and hardware keys like YubiKey that never expose secrets.

nodes.text: Smoking gun: history on a new device with no manual key transfer.

evidence.text: Smoking gun: can history move across devices without manual key transfer? Encryption means a public locker plus a receiver-only master key; a second device should not magically hold it. Signal forces key copying; any Facebook touch of the key equals a door-key copy on a public billboard.

nodes.text: WhatsApp server stores encrypted history and hands keys to devices it authenticates.

evidence.text: WhatsApp: server stores encrypted history plus account-to-device mappings; new devices are authenticated by the server and handed decryption keys. Safeguards (device lists, security codes) rely on honest server reporting, which could hide a rogue device.

nodes.text: Proton generates the private key in-browser, wrapping it with bcrypt and AES-256.

evidence.text: Proton: private key is generated in the browser, then encrypted with the user password using bcrypt and AES-256 before server storage. The encrypted private key lives on Proton servers, not only the original device.

nodes.text: Six-step login: type, bcrypt with server salt, authenticate, fetch key, decrypt locally, read.

evidence.text: Proton login in six steps: type password; browser bcrypt-hashes it with server-provided salt; hash goes to Proton for authentication; server returns the encrypted private key; browser decrypts it locally with the original password; mail becomes readable.

nodes.text: Hashing authenticates one-way; encryption protects two-way under the actual password.

evidence.text: Hashing (authentication) is one-way and irreversible; encryption (private-key protection) is two-way and reversible with the key. The key wraps in the actual password, not its hash.

nodes.text: In theory the seen hash cannot decrypt the password-wrapped key.

evidence.text: Theory: Proton sees only the hash for login, which should not decrypt the password-wrapped key.

nodes.text: Malicious client code could capture the typed password before hashing.

evidence.text: Proton residual risk: malicious client code (web app or update) could capture the typed password before hashing; with the stored encrypted key, that decrypts everything. Trust requires matching open-source code, no compelled future injection, uncompromised infrastructure.

nodes.text: Proton must steal the password first; WhatsApp grants keys directly.

evidence.text: Crucial difference: Proton lacks directly usable keys and must compromise the client first; WhatsApp's server can directly grant key access to any device it authenticates.

nodes.text: Signal: 30-digit passphrase file, device-to-device transfer, or unseen 64-character key.

evidence.text: Signal options: (1) Android manual local backup, an encrypted file guarded by a 30-digit passphrase, physically transferred; (2) direct device-to-device transfer with both present; (3) newer Secure Backups encrypted with a 64-character recovery key Signal never sees.

nodes.text: Zero-knowledge: no decryption, no recovery help after a lost key.

evidence.text: Signal servers can never grant history access; even cloud backups open only to the on-device recovery key. Genuinely zero-knowledge: no decryption, no recovery help if the key is lost.

evidence.text: Password layer: even trusted encryption leaves the plaintext-password question; with password plus encrypted key, everything decrypts.

nodes.text: Escrow (WhatsApp) versus password-wrapped (Proton) versus client-controlled (Signal).

evidence.text: Comparison table. Keys generated on-device for all three. Private keys: WhatsApp encrypted on servers with server-grantable keys (server-mediated escrow); Proton encrypted on servers by user password (password-encrypted storage); Signal on-device or under unseen recovery key (client-controlled). New device: WhatsApp server grants keys; Proton ships encrypted key for local decryption; Signal needs physical transfer or unseen 64-char key. Rogue device: YES for WhatsApp, NO for Proton (short of malicious client) and Signal. Trust and models as in ¶18.

evidence.text: Verifiable: open-source clients (hashing before sending, though silent on servers); Wireshark traffic inspection (plaintext over the wire is a flag, HTTPS hides server fate); audits (trusted auditor, trusted deployment).

nodes.text: Uncheckable: running code, later updates, rogue staff, breaches.

evidence.text: Unverifiable: closed server code (even shown code may not be running); later updates can add logging; rogue employees or breaches can inject it.

nodes.text: Good: open servers, audits, clean breaches; bad: reset-proof data, obscurity, violations.

evidence.text: Signals: good (open-source servers, published audits, clean breaches); bad (password reset preserving old data, security through obscurity, past privacy violations).

nodes.text: Facebook 2019: 200-600 million passwords, 20,000+ searchers, archives from 2012.

evidence.text: Cases: Adobe 2013 (plaintext hints aided brute force); Facebook 2019 (200-600 million plaintext passwords searchable by 20,000+ employees, some archives from 2012; claimed unintentional, no abuse found); small services (plaintext or unsalted MD5, discovered at breach).

evidence.text: Trust becomes unnecessary only if: all crypto is client-side (Signal-style recovery keys); the server sees nothing decryptable (zero-knowledge proofs); code is open, reproducibly built, and verifiably running.
